title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6797 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: India October CPI inflation rises to 6.09%, food inflation accelerates to 8.94%
body: India CPI Y/Y 6.09% vs 5.93% expected Prior 5.54% Full report India's CPI rose to 6.09% y/y in October, according to provisional data, pointing to increased price pressures in the economy. The headline inflation rate was higher in rural areas, where prices increased by 6.63% y/y, compared with 5.41% in urban areas. Food inflation was a big standout, with the Consumer Food Price Index rising 8.94% y/y in October. Food price increases were relatively broad-based across the country, with rural food inflation reaching 9.09% and urban food inflation standing at 8.68%. The figures highlight the significant contribution of food prices to India's inflationary pressures, with food inflation running well above the headline CPI rate. Overall, the October report points to a challenging inflation environment for the Reserve Bank of India. Given the acceleration in inflation, the market is pricing in a 69% chance of a 25 bps hike at the next RBI meeting, with 31% probabilitiy of a larger 50 bps move. The US-Iran war has been a major contributor of inflation through higher crude oil prices, increasing India's import bill and raising transportation, energy and agricultural production costs. As a major oil importer, India is particularly vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the Middle East. Higher energy and fertiliser costs gradually feed into consumer prices, while a weaker rupee also makes imports more expensive. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

title: Crude oil is caught between hopes of de-escalation and concerns of further escalation. What's next?
body: Crude oil has been consolidating around recent lows as the US-Iran uncertainty keeps traders guessing on the next move. The US-Iran conflict remains the main driver of course, with diplomatic efforts showing some signs of progress but no concrete breakthrough yet. Oil prices dipped yesterday after the Wall Street Journal reported that the US Vice President Vance was considering face-to-face talks with a top Iranian security official in an effort to end the war. However, significant mistrust remains, with Iranian officials accusing Washington of preparing further military strikes or tighter economic pressure. Iran has also continued to issue warnings of retaliation against US military bases and reportedly targeted ship navigation systems near the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the US military says its blockade has prevented Iran from exporting oil, while US forces are working to keep the Strait open to commercial shipping. The conflicting signals leave the outlook highly uncertain, with oil prices remaining sensitive to any developments that could either pave the way for de-escalation or trigger another escalation. It goes without saying that a concrete breakthrough would trigger a significant selloff and take oil prices back to pre-war levels relatively quickly.

title: Chart of the day: USD/JPY nears 160.00 as technical warning signs raise Japan intervention risks
body: Well, it looks like dollar bulls are starting to play with fire again. USD/JPY is creeping back towards the 160.00 level and while the move might look like another show of strength for the dollar, I suspect that Japanese authorities aren't finding it quite as amusing. And from a technical perspective, there are reasons why Tokyo officials might be getting a tad bit nervous this week. After spending much of October repeatedly struggling to really test the 159.00 level and with repeated failed attempts in getting above the 200-day moving average (blue line), USD/JPY has finally pushed past those key resistance levels. Buyers had been knocking on the same door for weeks but are now finally managing a breakthrough. And with price pushing past both the key daily moving averages in the latest run higher, the technical picture is threatening to open up towards 160.00 next. However, this is where things start to get a little more dicey for USD/JPY and dollar bulls. The 160.00 mark isn't just another technical level. These sort of big psychological barriers and figure levels are often a potential trigger point for Japanese authorities to step up their intervention warnings or even potentially act outright. This was precisely where we saw intervention action back during late April and early May. And with USD/JPY now approaching that territory again, the technical break above 159.00 provides a rather clear reason for Tokyo officials to worry about the yen's renewed depreciation.

title: Bitcoin consolidates near recent lows as hawkish Fed repricing weighs on the crypto market
body: Bitcoin has been mostly consolidating around recent lows as the hawkish repricing triggered by Fed governor Waller's remarks and the hot US CPI weighed on the crypto market. As a reminder, Fed's Waller not only said he would support a rate hike in December regardless of the inflation data but also raised the possibility of a larger 50 bps move if inflation comes in hotter than expected. Sure enough, the US CPI data came in above expectations and increased the probabilities of 50 bps hike. Following the CPI data, Fed's Hammack also left a door open for a larger rate increase. Traders are currently pricing in just a 12% probability of a 50 bps hike, but those odds could climb further if more Fed officials endorse the possibility or refrain from pushing back against it. Meanwhile, US-Iran negotiations remain in a deadlock. The WSJ reported that US Vice President Vance is considering holding face-to-face talks with a senior Iranian security official in an attempt to bring the conflict to an end. However, separate reports suggested that senior Iranian officials believe Washington is preparing either further military strikes or tighter economic pressure in an attempt to provoke a response from Tehran. There is clearly still a significant amount of mistrust between the two sides, reinforcing the view that a diplomatic breakthrough may not be as near as market expected. Looking ahead, Bitcoin will likely remain under pressure amid the negative macro backdrop.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran negotiations remain at a stalemate. The central bank's resident dove is once again preaching caution, warning that further tightening could undermine the progress that Japan has made in achieving sustainable inflation. Here are his latest remarks from today: Inflation has already reached roughly 2%, leaving little reason to push prices higher BOJ must be cautious about raising interest rates too quickly Further rate hikes may be necessary in the future, but should be carried out slowly Not opposed to raising rates altogether and is not considering proposing a rate cut Japan's neutral interest rate may be somewhat above the current policy rate Has no specific terminal interest rate in mind Policy decisions should be assessed at every meeting, considering economic risks and financial conditions BOJ could still raise or lower rates even after reaching a level consistent with its inflation target BOJ does not directly control exchange rates (declines to specify a desirable USD/JPY level) Further tightening risks weakening underlying inflation, particularly as consumption continues to lack momentum Now, I wouldn't read too much into the dovish undertones here. title: Chinese tech firms reportedly rushing to secure more Nvidia chip capacity amid fears that spy scandal would spur tighter restrictions
body: Well, talk about a scandal sending everyone scrambling for the exits. Except in this case, Chinese tech firms aren't exactly looking to leave the party. Instead, they're trying to grab as much Nvidia computing power as they can before Washington potentially slams the door shut. Reuters is reporting that AI companies in China are looking to secure more Nvidia-powered cloud computing capacity at overseas data centres, fearing that the controversy surrounding CEO Jensen Huang could accelerate tougher US restrictions, citing three people familiar with the matter. The sources noted that a major Chinese cloud provider has reportedly discussed locking in overseas capacity, while smaller AI firms are exploring similar arrangements - particularly in Southeast Asia. And there's good reason that Chinese tech firms are getting nervous here. For some context, the US already restricts China's access to Nvidia's most advanced AI chips. However, these companies have been able to work around some of those restrictions by renting computing power from data centres outside the country. The fear now is that at some point, that very loophole could soon become a casualty of the latest political fallout. Essentially, Huang's latest affair scandal and controversy with a woman who is suspected to be a Chinese spy has given lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for tighter export controls.

title: Heads up: UK September GDP in focus but will weak growth really stop the BOE from hiking again?
body: The UK September monthly and latest quarterly GDP report are due at 0700 GMT today and the question that markets will be asking is just how bad would the numbers have to be to convince the BOE to take its foot off the rate hike pedal? The estimates are pointing to a flat reading after the economy expanded by just 0.1% in August. And that follows from the more encouraging 0.4% increase in July, suggesting that growth momentum is becoming rather uneven in the past quarter. That being said, the bigger picture isn't quite as soft as the latest monthly numbers might suggest. The UK economy expanded by 0.7% in the three months to August, largely supported by services activity. Meanwhile, manufacturing and construction have also been keeping pace, albeit less convincingly. Besides the monthly figures, we'll also be getting the preliminary Q3 GDP estimate. So, that should ffer a better sense of whether the economy is holding up or starting to buckle under the weight of higher borrowing costs and surging energy prices. The latter have seen some better developments in the past week but will still need time to filter through back to the economy. At the balance, a downside surprise in the numbers could weigh on sterling and temper expectations for further BOE tightening. But unless we see a particularly ugly set of numbers, I reckon that today's report will do little to materially change up the BOE's plans for December at this juncture.

That matters most for USD/JPY, which is already near the 160 area where Japan has stepped up verbal warnings. Higher long-end yields would also weigh on gold, which has slipped below $4,000, and add pressure on richly valued tech stocks already hit by the Nvidia leadership shock. Oil is the key risk to the call. A sustained fall in crude would ease inflation fears and could cap yields, while a renewed rise linked to the Iran war would reinforce the move higher. --- Cheaper oil might give Treasuries a breather, but CBA thinks growth and a hawkish Fed will keep pushing the 10-year yield higher. title: ANZ says RBA hike bets have cooled, but 3.7% core inflation will keep it cautious
body: Cooler RBA hike expectations take away one source of support for the Australian dollar, at a time when US yields are rising and the Fed is on a hiking path. That leaves the AUD exposed to further dollar strength. Sticky services inflation should limit how far Australian rate expectations can fall, though, which caps the downside for front-end bond yields. Lower oil prices help Australian headline inflation but do little for the domestic services pressures ANZ is focused on, so the RBA's cautious stance looks likely to persist. --- Growth is cooling, but services inflation isn't, and that keeps the RBA from relaxing even as the case for another hike fades. title: US 30-year bond auction tails as demand disappoints for second straight day
body: High yield 5.441% vs 5.437% WI Tail of 0.4 basis points Bid-to-cover 2.36x vs 2.44x average Dealers awarded 11.39% vs 9.49% average The US Treasury sold $25 billion in 30-year bonds on Thursday in a disappointing auction that adds to signs of softening demand at the long end of the curve. The auction stopped at 5.441%, a 0.4 basis point tail compared to the 5.437% when-issued yield. That's a deterioration from last month's 0.1 basis point tail and compares unfavourably with the six-auction average of a 0.1 basis point stop-through. The bid-to-cover ratio fell to 2.36x from 2.54x previously, also below the 2.44x six-auction average. The breakdown of buyers wasn't particularly encouraging either. Indirect bidders, which include foreign central banks and other institutional investors, took 68.11%, down from 72.32% last month and below the 70.49% average. Dealers were left holding 11.39%, up sharply from 6.79% in the previous auction. Direct bidders took 20.5%, roughly in line with recent averages. The results follow Tuesday's soft 10-year auction and suggest that investors remain reluctant to aggressively add duration, even after yields cheapened ahead of the sale. The good news is that the high yield was well below last month's 5.618%, but that's more a reflection of the broader rally in bonds than stronger underlying demand. The takeaway is another weak auction, with the higher dealer allocation particularly troubling.

That first line is the one that matters. Stimulus is a demand word. For two years the Fed's framing on AI was about supply: productivity, capacity, a disinflationary tailwind somewhere down the road. Goolsbee is now describing it the way you'd describe a fiscal package. It's an extension of what he's been saying for a month. In October he said inflation was starting to feel like aggregate overheating, with data center costs spilling into the broader economy. On Monday he said the build-out increasingly resembled traditional demand overheating, the kind central banks need to hit aggressively up front. Then came Tuesday's CPI. Headline prices rose 0.4% in October and core rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Waller said he would consider voting for 50 bps in December and Logan wants at least two more hikes. At some point it will turn but we're not there yet. For background, the National Association of Realtors publishes its existing home sales report monthly at 10 am ET, usually in the third or fourth week of the following month. Existing homes make up roughly 90% of US home sales, so the report is the broadest monthly read on housing market activity. The headline figure is the seasonally adjusted annualized rate of sales, covering single-family homes, townhomes, condominiums and co-ops. Because the data count closed transactions, they reflect contracts signed one to two months earlier. NAR's pending home sales index, released later each month, tracks contract signings and gives an earlier signal of where closings are headed. The report also includes the median existing-home price, which isn't seasonally adjusted and is usually compared with the same month a year earlier. Because it's a median, it can be skewed by changes in the mix of homes selling, such as more high-end sales in a given month. Repeat-sales measures like Case-Shiller give a cleaner read on price trends. Inventory is one of the most closely watched details. NAR reports the number of homes for sale and months' supply, the time it would take to sell current inventory at the current sales pace.

title: US weekly initial jobless claims 200K vs 195K expected
body: Prior was 189K Four week average vs 194.75K prior Continuing claims vs 1710K expected The US Department of Labor publishes its weekly unemployment insurance claims report every Thursday at 8:30 am ET, or Wednesday when a holiday falls later in the week. It's the most timely official read on the US labor market, covering the week that ended just five days earlier. The headline figure is initial jobless claims, the number of people filing for unemployment benefits for the first time. It's a direct gauge of layoffs. Because the weekly data are noisy, markets also watch the four-week moving average to gauge the trend. The report also includes continuing claims, the number of people still receiving benefits after their initial filing, which lags initial claims by a week. While initial claims track layoffs, continuing claims show how hard it is for people out of work to find new jobs. A steady rise in continuing claims alongside low initial claims has often signaled a "low-hire, low-fire" labor market where workers aren't being let go but are struggling to get rehired. Claims tend to get extra attention during the week that includes the 12th of the month, which is the survey reference week for the monthly nonfarm payrolls report, giving an early hint at the jobs data. Seasonal adjustment is a persistent challenge. Holidays, summer auto plant retooling, school calendars, hurricanes and strikes can distort the numbers, as can surges in fraudulent filings in individual states.

title: Why markets sometimes ignore economic data
body: Key economic releases are among the most closely watched events in financial markets. Inflation figures, employment reports, business surveys and so on can all influence expectations for monetary policy and the macroeconomic outlook. Yet, markets do not always react to the data in the same way. The key thing to understand is that financial markets are forward-looking. Asset prices reflect expectations about future economic conditions, central bank decisions and so on. It's never about the present conditions. The market reaction to an economic release depends on whether it changes the underlying expectations. Not every economic release carries the same importance. For example, a stronger than expected employment report might initially push bond yields higher. However, if inflation is simultaneously declining and the central bank is becoming more concerned about missing the inflation target, the employment surprise might not be enough to change expectations for interest rates. The opposite can also happen. A relatively small inflation surprise could have a significant impact if markets think that it's going to change the central bank's next move. Central banks generally determine which data matters most Policymakers monitor a wide range of economic indicators, but the relative importance of each variable changes depending on the economic context.

title: How IPOs work: The process of bringing a company to the stock market
body: An Initial Public Offering (IPO) is the process through which a privately held company offers its shares to the public for the first time and becomes listed on a stock exchange. An IPO allows a company to raise capital from a broader pool of investors while giving the public an opportunity to participate in its growth. Before going public, ownership is generally concentrated among founders, employees, venture capital funds and other private investors. An IPO changes this by creating a public market where institutional and retail investors can buy and sell shares. Companies go public to raise capital for expansion, research, acquisitions or debt reduction. An IPO can also provide liquidity to existing shareholders, increase the company's visibility and make it easier to use publicly traded shares for acquisitions or employee compensation. How does an IPO work? The IPO process usually begins with the company appointing investment banks, known as underwriters, to manage the offering. These banks help determine the company's valuation, structure the transaction, prepare the regulatory documentation and market the shares to potential investors. In the US, companies generally file a registration statement called Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This document provides detailed information about the company's business model, financial performance, risks, management and intended use of the proceeds.

title: How could Japan shake up the global markets?
body: How could Japan shake up the global markets? Minutes from the Bank of Japan's October meeting point to another rate hike in December, and it's easy to see why. The weak yen and rising energy costs driven by Middle East tensions have pushed core inflation to 2.1% year over year in September, its highest level since early 2026 and above the BOJ's 2% target, while the measure excluding food and energy climbed to 2.4%. Higher oil prices add to these inflationary pressures, particularly because Japan relies heavily on energy imports. This also makes oil prices an important factor to watch when assessing the BOJ's next policy move. As for why the BOJ is holding back, even though the conditions for a hike are already in place, a tighter policy could help bring inflation under control and ease pressure on the yen, but it would also make borrowing more expensive, potentially cooling business activity and investment. Another reason is Japan's massive government debt, which exceeds 200% of GDP. Rather than paying it off, the government keeps rolling over maturing bonds by issuing new ones, while continuing to pay interest on its debt. This means that higher rates would make that debt increasingly expensive to service, putting even more pressure on public finances and raising concerns about long-term debt sustainability. Currency intervention could also help ease some of this pressure.

title: Connecting the dots: Why falling oil prices might not deliver the inflation relief everyone expects
body: Oil prices are starting to fall again, so surely that must mean our cost-of-living problems should be disappearing too, right? Well, if only the economics behind that were so straightforward and cooperative. WTI crude has dropped back to just below $86 today amid hopes of easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. That is welcome news for households especially after the energy shock this year and I can understand why markets are getting excited as well. But before popping the champagne, this is something worth remembering. Cheaper oil doesn't necessarily mean cheaper living. Sure, lower oil prices should eventually bring some relief to let's say the gasoline pump. That means transportation and shipping costs could also ease, affording businesses a little bit more breathing room. But here's something to think about. When was the last time that your rent, insurance bill or favourite restaurant actually became cheaper? Dum, dum, dum. Exactly. And this is precisely where the inflation story gets a little more complicated beyond just falling oil prices. Just take a look at the chart above. Since January 2020, gasoline prices have jumped by nearly 68% while food and shelter costs have risen by around 35% and 34% respectively in the US. Meanwhile, overall consumer prices have increased by roughly 31%. Now, here's the interesting bit. Nominal wages have also risen by nearly 34% during the same period, slightly outpacing overall inflation.

title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, November 13, 2026 - NY Fed's Williams on the agenda
body: New York Fed President John Williams will take part in a panel discussion at 6.30pm US Eastern time on Thursday (2330 GMT), at a UC Berkeley Alumni Salon event in New York. The format matters. This is a moderated panel at an alumni event rather than a set-piece policy speech, so there may be no prepared text. Anything that moves markets is more likely to come from questions on the outlook than from scripted remarks. The timing is hard to ignore, though. Williams is a permanent FOMC voter and the committee's vice chair. He speaks two days after a hotter-than-expected October CPI report. Headline prices rose 0.4% on the month against a 0.3% forecast, and core rose 0.3% against 0.2% expected. The BLS did not publish 12-month rates because of the lapse in government funding. Markets repriced quickly. After the release, CME FedWatch put the odds of a 25 basis point hike at the 9 December decision at around 85% to 90%. Before the data the odds of a 50bp move were close to zero; afterwards they rose to roughly 10% to 15%. A half-point hike is still unlikely, and some analysts call it a high bar, but it is now being discussed. Fed Governor Waller has said he would favour a quarter-point hike in December and could prefer a half-point if inflation runs hotter than expected.
